newsitem.title: UK: UK's Blair gives go-ahead to millennium dome.
newsitem.headline: UK's Blair gives go-ahead to millennium dome.

text.p: Prime Minister Tony Blair, saying he was following his instincts in defiance of a tide of adverse media comment, gave the go-ahead on Thursday to a futuristic exhibition near London to mark the dawning of the millennium.

Saying the project would put Britain "firmly on the map" internationally and boost the country's morale, Blair won his cabinet over to the controversial exhibition which many believed was doomed, a close aide said.
"He fully understands the arguments against, but he felt there are times when leaders have to follow their instincts," said the aide from the prime minister's Downing Street office.

But Blair set five tough new tests that must be met by the organisers of the exhibition, built around a huge steel dome designed by Lord Richard Rogers, the architect of France's Pompidou Centre, at Greenwich on the bank of the Thames.

It had to leave a lasting legacy for future generations, there could be no extra public spending, more work had to be done on the concept behind it, people from all over the country had to be involved and there had to be a management shake-up.
But the aide made it clear the project was set to go ahead. "When he (Blair) is committed to something, he makes things happen," he said.
Government officials said that if the project had been cancelled, 30 to 50 million pounds which has already been spent by the government and private investors would have been lost.

So far the government has spent between 10 to 20 million pounds on reclaiming the derelict, polluted site for the exhibition. Around 200 million pounds of National Lottery money has also been promised, but the bulk of the money will still have to come from private industry.
The project was thought up by Conservative deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine who wanted it built by private industry with help from the National Lottery.
But Labour's lukewarm support before the May 1 election which swept it to power meant private companies did not sign up.
Amid increasing confusion and delay, estimated costs spiralled towards one billion pounds ($1.64 billion).
Just before the election Labour demanded cuts as the price for its support. The budget came down to 580 million pounds.
But fierce opposition to the project, and in particular the dome, continued with the mass-selling Sun newspaper running a campaign to dump what it called the "daft" scheme.
Commentators and building experts have expressed doubts the exhibition can be completed on time to welcome the millennium.
Blair's aide said the key task now was to win over the media. "He (Blair) has never been averse to swimming against the tide of opinion and turning that opinion in his favour," he said.
The prime minister, who called in the election campaign for voters to give him 1,000 days to prepare for 1,000 years, wants the exhibition to be "Britain's window to the future".
He also wants to link it to his key themes of job creation and education, with the exhibition acting as a catalyst for the development of new technologies in Britain.
